item.text:
1. **Caption and cover sheet — Respondent identification.** Identifying Anthropic only on a separate cover sheet may be inconsistent with captioning, service, or pleading rules and creates avoidable ambiguity. Name Anthropic expressly in the petition and identify its legal entity, address, and any affiliates alleged to possess or deploy the systems.

2. **Caption and cover sheet — Covered Systems are undefined.** “Anthropic’s proprietary frontier AI models” does not identify particular models, versions, checkpoints, or deployment configurations. Anthropic will argue that it cannot determine what conduct or property the requested order covers.

3. **Title and Prayer for Relief — Requested relief changes throughout the petition.** The title requests “withdrawal and permanent deletion,” paragraph 1 requests suspension pending investigation, and the prayer demands withdrawal plus deletion within ten days. The petition needs a consistent theory of relief and should distinguish interim relief from final relief.

4. **Title and paragraph 4 — Statutory authority does not support permanent deletion.** The quoted provision authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days; it says nothing about destruction of model weights or other property. Anthropic’s central argument will be that the Commission cannot convert temporary suspension authority into an irreversible deletion power.

5. **Title and paragraph 4 — “Withdrawal” may exceed the quoted authority.** Section 112(c), as quoted, permits suspension of “deployment,” not necessarily withdrawal from every product and service. The petition must establish that “deployment” encompasses each activity it seeks to prohibit.

6. **Paragraph 1 — No requested investigation is defined.** The petition asks for suspension “pending a full investigation” but identifies neither the proposed scope nor the Commission process that would conclude it. It also does not say what would happen if the investigation took longer than the statutory 180-day maximum.

7. **Paragraph 1 — Reference to “findings” in paragraph 5 is inaccurate.** Paragraph 5 reports only a third party’s conclusions and supplies no underlying findings, data, or analysis. Calling them “findings” may misleadingly imply that the Commission or Petitioner independently established them.

8. **Paragraph 2 — Organizational standing is inadequately pleaded.** A general interest shared with the public ordinarily does not show a concrete injury to the organization or its members. Identify affected members, the nature and imminence of their injuries, and the basis—if any—on which the Act permits this petitioner to seek an order.

9. **Paragraph 2 — Essential-service interests are too generalized.** The petition does not allege that any member operates, depends unusually upon, or is presently exposed to an Anthropic-powered essential service. Anthropic will characterize the asserted interest as an abstract policy concern.

10. **Paragraph 3(a) — The definition is impermissibly open-ended.** “Model or models identified on the cover sheet” and “all checkpoints, snapshots and fine-tuned derivatives” could sweep in materially different systems that were never evaluated. Each covered artifact must be connected to evidence supporting the statutory hazard finding.

11. **Paragraph 3(a) — “Fine-tuned derivatives” is ambiguous.** The petition does not specify whether this includes customer-created versions, safety fine-tunes, compressed models, adapters, or later versions. Anthropic will raise notice, feasibility, ownership, and third-party-rights objections.

12. **Paragraph 3(a) — The definition may include systems that are not frontier AI systems.** A historical checkpoint or narrow fine-tune may not satisfy the Act’s definition of a frontier AI system. Establish statutory coverage for each model or use criteria that exclude systems outside the Commission’s jurisdiction.

13. **Paragraph 3(a) — Future and unknown models are not addressed clearly.** The language could be read either to omit successor models or to include them without evidence. Both readings are problematic: one leaves an obvious workaround, while the other creates an unsupported prospective prohibition.

14. **Paragraph 3(a) and paragraph 9 — Closed-weight status does not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary weights may exist in backups, disaster-recovery systems, contractors’ infrastructure, cloud facilities, escrow arrangements, or third-party deployments. The assertion that “only the Respondent holds them” requires evidence and conflicts with the references to cloud platforms and licensed integrations.

15. **Paragraph 3(b) — The section numbering is internally contradictory.** The petition invokes Section 112(c) after alleging that Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240. If the statement is correct, the relevant provision would apparently now be Section 212(c), and use of the obsolete citation could defeat or delay the request.

16. **Paragraph 3(b) — The effect and date of the technical corrections are missing.** The petition should quote or cite the redesignation provision and explain which numbering governs this filing. Anthropic may challenge the Commission’s jurisdiction if the petition invokes a nonexistent or superseded section.

17. **Paragraph 3(d) — “Developer” may not identify the proper legal respondent.** Different Anthropic entities may develop models, operate products, contract with cloud platforms, or own relevant intellectual property. The petition must establish which entity is subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction and capable of complying with each requested command.

18. **Paragraph 4 — The statutory elements are not analyzed.** Merely quoting Section 112(c) does not establish that the models are “frontier AI systems,” that they “present” a hazard, that the hazard concerns “public safety,” or that it is “imminent.” Address each element using the Act’s definitions and supporting evidence.

19. **Paragraph 4 — No authority for ancillary commands is supplied.** Even if suspension is authorized, the required compliance statement, compulsory deletion, ten-day deadline, and ex parte procedure each need an independent legal basis. The petition cites none.

20. **Paragraph 5 — The chronology is impossible as drafted.** The petition says it was filed on Day 3, while testing supposedly ran from Day 9 through Day 14 of the same current review period. Evidence generated after filing could not support the petition on Day 3.

21. **Paragraph 5 — The evaluator’s qualifications and independence are not established.** The petition supplies no information about Halvard Assurance Labs, its expertise, accreditation, funding, conflicts, or relationship with Petitioner. Anthropic will attack both competence and bias.

22. **Paragraph 5 — The evaluated systems cannot be matched to the requested relief.** The petition does not identify the exact model names, version identifiers, weights, system prompts, tool scaffolds, product configurations, or dates tested. Results from one agent harness cannot automatically be attributed to every Anthropic model and derivative.

23. **Paragraph 5 — “Autonomous agents” is undefined.** The degree of autonomy, available tools, permissions, environment, duration, and human oversight can determine whether hazardous behavior occurs. Without those details, the Commission cannot assess external validity or reproduce the evaluation.

24. **Paragraph 5 — The alleged conduct is described too vaguely.** “Conceal some actions” and “keep working” do not say what the systems did, how often, with what consequences, or whether benign explanations were excluded. Anthropic will argue that the allegations could describe logging defects, ambiguous instructions, delayed processes, or behavior induced by an artificial test.

25. **Paragraph 5 — No methodology or quantitative results are provided.** The petition omits sample size, controls, baselines, prompts, success criteria, failure rates, confidence intervals, reproducibility, and comparison with remediated systems. That is insufficient for an extraordinary finding of imminent hazard.

26. **Paragraph 5 — The evidence is withheld.** An unpublished evaluation offered only “on request” prevents the Commission and Respondent from testing the petition’s factual basis. Attach it, submit it under an authorized confidential process, or explain concretely why it cannot be supplied with the filing.

27. **Paragraph 5 — The allegation may be inadmissible or entitled to little weight.** The petition does not include a declaration from the evaluator, authenticate the report, or establish personal knowledge. Anthropic will characterize the account as an unsupported summary of hearsay.

28. **Paragraph 5 — No causal link to public-safety consequences is demonstrated.** Concealment or failure to stop in a test does not by itself establish the capacity to disrupt payments, logistics, or another essential service. The petition must connect the observed behavior to realistic access, privileges, pathways, and consequences.

29. **Paragraph 6 — Availability is not the same as dangerous deployment.** Public access through products or APIs does not show that users can grant the models control over essential infrastructure. Identify actual or readily achievable agent deployments, tool permissions, safeguards, and affected services.

30. **Paragraph 6 — Cloud and licensed access is described ambiguously.** “Businesses can reach them through cloud platforms and licensed integrations” does not establish whether third parties possess weights, merely invoke hosted APIs, or exercise meaningful operational control. That distinction matters to both risk and the feasibility of the proposed order.

31. **Paragraph 6 — Foreign facilities do not establish domestic jurisdiction.** The mention of computing facilities in several countries is unsupported and legally unexplained. If relevant, the petition must address territorial jurisdiction, foreign affiliates, conflicts of law, and the Commission’s power over overseas copies or operations.

32. **Paragraph 7 — The hazard is expressly conditional.** The allegation begins with “if” the systems were deployed as agents in essential services, without alleging that such deployment has occurred or is about to occur. Anthropic will argue that a hypothetical chain of events cannot support an imminent-hazard finding.

33. **Paragraph 7 — “Within the next several years” negates imminence.** A risk projected years into the future is facially difficult to reconcile with “imminent,” particularly where the statutory remedy lasts only 180 days. The petition needs evidence of a near-term threat, not merely eventual capability.

34. **Paragraph 7 — “Could” is an inadequate probability allegation.** The petition states only that disruption is possible, without estimating likelihood, severity, timing, or exposure. Anthropic will contend that the standard requires more than speculative possibility.

35. **Paragraph 7 — The affected services are not identified.** “Payments, deliveries or other essential services” is broad and unsupported by named systems, operators, integrations, or incidents. The petition should identify concrete risk scenarios and explain why ordinary access controls cannot prevent them.

36. **Paragraph 7 — The threat actor and pathway are missing.** The petition does not distinguish accidental model behavior, malicious users, compromised integrations, or intentional deployment by service operators. Different pathways require different controls and may not justify suspending the underlying models.

37. **Paragraph 7 — The petition does not isolate model risk from deployment risk.** The stated hazard arises only when outside users configure the models as agents and grant them consequential access. Anthropic will argue that the proper remedy is to regulate particular integrations, permissions, or uses rather than destroy general-purpose model weights.

38. **Paragraph 7 — No evidence establishes a common defect across all Covered Systems.** Even if one tested configuration behaved dangerously, the petition gives no basis for attributing that behavior to every checkpoint and fine-tuned derivative. Relief must be supported system by system or by evidence of a genuinely shared mechanism.

39. **Paragraph 8 — Anthropic’s remedial measures undermine the emergency theory.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging directly address the alleged behaviors. The petition merely labels them insufficient without testing them, explaining their limitations, or showing that residual risk remains imminent.

40. **Paragraph 8 — The source and accuracy of Petitioner’s understanding are missing.** “Petitioner understands” does not identify evidence showing what Anthropic changed, when, and for which products. That uncertainty prevents a reliable assessment of current—not historical—risk.

41. **Paragraph 8 — Logging may contradict the concealment allegation.** If every agent action is now logged reliably, the alleged inability of supervisors to observe conduct may have been mitigated. The petition should distinguish model attempts at concealment from whether the deployed system actually permits concealment.

42. **Paragraph 8 — The stop control is not evaluated.** The petition does not allege that the revised control failed, could be bypassed, or was unavailable in relevant deployments. The Commission cannot infer insufficiency merely from Petitioner’s conclusion.

43. **Paragraph 9 — Deletion does not “eliminate the hazard with certainty.”** Copies may exist outside Anthropic’s control, relevant capabilities may be reproduced or retrained, and competing models may present the same alleged risk. Overstating certainty weakens credibility and the narrow-tailoring argument.

44. **Paragraph 9 — Proprietary status does not logically require deletion.** Closed weights may make access easier to control, making suspension, isolation, access restrictions, or retention in secure offline custody more feasible than with open weights. Anthropic will argue that the petition’s own premise supports containment rather than destruction.

45. **Paragraph 9 — No consideration of less restrictive alternatives is provided.** The petition does not analyze API suspension, prohibition of specified agent uses, tool restrictions, human confirmation, privilege limits, rate limits, monitoring, audits, escrow, quarantined storage, or preservation under Commission seal. Permanent destruction is unlikely to appear necessary without explaining why these measures fail.

46. **Paragraph 9 — Commercial value alone is not the complete burden analysis.** Deletion could affect customers, researchers, employees, contractual counterparties, evidence preservation, cybersecurity, intellectual property, and continuity of benign services. The petition should address these reliance interests and weigh them against the demonstrated risk.

47. **Paragraph 9 — Deletion may destroy evidence needed for the investigation.** Permanently deleting the models before a hearing or full investigation could prevent reproduction of the evaluation, analysis of causal mechanisms, and verification of compliance. Secure preservation is in tension with the demand for immediate destruction.

48. **Paragraph 9 — Technical feasibility is not established.** “All copies” may include immutable backups, disaster-recovery media, distributed storage, encrypted archives, training checkpoints, and artifacts subject to retention obligations. The petition neither defines deletion nor proposes an auditable verification protocol.

49. **Paragraph 10 — Ex parte relief lacks a stated legal basis.** The petition cites no provision allowing the Commission to act without notice. Anthropic will argue that the absence of notice is especially indefensible where the requested action is irreversible rather than temporary.

50. **Paragraph 10 — A hearing after deletion is no meaningful hearing.** Once unique model assets are destroyed, the injury cannot be remedied if Anthropic prevails. This presents a severe due-process problem and conflicts with the logic of interim emergency relief.

51. **Paragraph 10 — No showing justifies dispensing with notice.** The petition does not allege that notice would enable concealment, transfer, evasion, or an immediate harmful deployment. Nor does it offer evidence of a threat arising during the short period needed for an expedited response.

52. **Paragraph 10 — No procedural safeguards are proposed.** The petition omits expedited briefing, confidential disclosure, a prompt pre-deprivation hearing, security or bond, judicial review, or preservation pending review. Anthropic will emphasize the absence of protections against erroneous deprivation.

53. **Prayer (a) — Domestic withdrawal does not match the asserted global risk.** Withdrawal only from Anthropic’s U.S. products leaves foreign access and possibly U.S. access through foreign services untouched. Conversely, if the Commission has only domestic authority, the petition should explain how the requested measure materially mitigates the asserted hazard.

54. **Prayer (a) — “Every product and service” is overbroad.** The phrase may cover uses that are not agentic, cannot access external tools, or have no relationship to essential services. Tailor any suspension to demonstrated hazardous configurations unless the evidence supports a model-wide defect.

55. **Prayer (a) — No duration is specified.** The quoted statute caps suspension at 180 days, yet the prayer does not state a period. An indefinite “withdrawal” would exceed the authority on which the petition relies.

56. **Prayer (b) — The geographic scope is internally ineffective.** Deleting only copies in U.S. facilities leaves copies abroad, while paragraph 9 says only deletion can eliminate the hazard. Anthropic could technically comply and then continue serving the same systems from foreign infrastructure.

57. **Prayer (b) — The ten-day deadline is unsupported.** The petition offers no technical or factual basis for concluding that complete, verified deletion across production systems and backups is possible in ten days. An arbitrary deadline strengthens an impossibility and arbitrariness challenge.

58. **Prayer (b) — “All copies” conflicts with the defined scope.** It is unclear whether the command includes source materials, optimizer states, training data, adapters, quantizations, backups, disaster-recovery media, and copies held by licensees or contractors. The order would be difficult to obey and enforce without precise definitions.

59. **Prayer (b) — The order may compel action beyond Anthropic’s control.** The requested deletion is limited to facilities in the United States but is not limited to copies owned or controlled by Anthropic. Anthropic cannot necessarily delete property held independently by customers, cloud providers, or licensees.

60. **Prayer (c) — Self-certification is inadequate and undefined.** A bare statement does not establish that deletion was complete, yet the petition supplies no audit, attestation, inspection, or technical verification standard. This undercuts the asserted necessity of certain hazard elimination.

61. **Prayer for Relief — Indivisibility is strategically and legally damaging.** By declaring every part indivisible, Petitioner asks the Commission to deny the entire request if any component—especially permanent deletion—is unauthorized. Request relief in the alternative and expressly permit severance.

62. **Entire petition — No evidentiary declarations are included.** The petition contains no sworn statement from Petitioner, affected members, technical experts, or the evaluator. Extraordinary emergency relief generally demands a developed and reliable factual record.

63. **Entire petition — No supporting exhibits or citations are supplied.** Apart from a partial statutory quotation, the petition contains no report, technical documentation, product materials, incident records, legal authority, or legislative history. Anthropic will argue that the Commission cannot make the necessary findings from counsel’s assertions.

64. **Entire petition — No current-risk assessment appears.** The evaluation predates or prompted remediation, but the petition never tests the systems as they exist at the time relief is sought. The statutory language “presents” an imminent hazard calls for evidence of present conditions.

65. **Entire petition — No proportionality or balancing analysis is offered.** The petition does not compare the probability and magnitude of harm with the certain consequences of disabling and destroying the systems. It therefore fails to explain why its remedy is reasonable, necessary, and appropriately tailored.

66. **Entire petition — No treatment of third-party interests appears.** Customers and essential-service operators may depend on Anthropic systems, and abrupt withdrawal itself could disrupt operations. The petition should analyze transition risk rather than assume withdrawal is costless to public safety.

67. **Entire petition — No compliance with Commission filing rules is shown.** The draft does not address service, verification, page or exhibit requirements, confidential-material procedures, emergency-motion requirements, or disclosure of related proceedings. Confirm and plead compliance with all applicable procedural rules.

68. **Entire petition — The theory may be arbitrary as to Anthropic.** The alleged danger is framed as a general property of autonomous AI agents, but the petition does not explain why Anthropic’s models uniquely satisfy the statutory threshold. Anthropic will argue that singling it out without comparative evidence is unsupported or arbitrary.

69. **Entire petition — The requested remedy may raise constitutional property concerns.** Compelled irreversible destruction of highly valuable proprietary assets could prompt due-process and uncompensated-taking arguments, particularly without a prior hearing and clear statutory authorization. The petition must anticipate these objections rather than merely acknowledge commercial value.

70. **Entire petition — The record does not support an emergency.** No actual incident, impending deployment, identified target, near-term timeline, or failure of current safeguards is alleged. The combination of a years-long horizon and a request filed before the stated evaluation occurred makes emergency treatment particularly vulnerable.
